paras: The New York City race riot of August 1900 was a night of attacks on Black people by white crowds on Manhattan's West Side on August 15-16, set off by the death of Policeman Robert J. Thorpe, who had been stabbed during an arrest. Dozens of Black men were beaten or clubbed and Lloyd Lee was shot by a policeman, but no deaths were reported. Papers compared it with the recent New Orleans riot, and the conduct of the police, accused of joining the attacks, dominated later coverage.

Thorpe, a plainclothes patrolman, arrested May Enoch for loitering at Eighth Avenue and Forty-first Street early on August 12. According to the New-York Tribune, Arthur Harris, who lived with Enoch, intervened and was alleged to have stabbed Thorpe, who died on August 13.

On the night of August 15 a crowd collected at Thorpe's home on Ninth Avenue, where his body lay. Shortly before 11 o'clock, the Tribune reported, a drunken woman cried that Black people "ought to be kilt," and white men beat a passing Black youth. The crowd, put at several hundred and then 1,500 or more, then attacked Black people "regardless of age or sex" from Twenty-ninth to Forty-second Street.

Black passengers were dragged from streetcars and beaten, and tenement residents threw bricks at the crowd and police, who fired into the windows. Nathan Arlington was pulled from his bicycle and beaten while, observers said, nearby policemen did nothing. John B. Mallory, a student, was beaten and then clubbed by a policeman, and the performer George Walker was pulled from a car and escaped into a hotel. A wire report said one man survived an attempted lynching only because "there was no good place to fasten the rope."

Lee was shot and clubbed near Seventh Avenue and Thirty-seventh Street and arrested on a charge of stabbing Detective John Kennedy; he said a policeman had shot him. Chief Devery brought in hundreds of reserves and closed the saloons, and order returned after 3 a.m. Estimates of the injured ran from fifty to "sixty or perhaps a hundred" Black people, with a dozen whites hurt.

Of nineteen prisoners arraigned on August 16 only four were white, and Magistrate Cornell blamed "poor white trash" and censured the police. An off-duty patrolman accused of leading a crowd against Black people was suspended and fined $10.

On August 20 a meeting at the Mount Olivet Baptist parsonage raised $1,000 to hire counsel and seek the removal of Devery and Acting Captain Cooney. Henry J. Down reported that Inspector Thompson called him "one of those smart niggers," and Alfred A. Akins swore that he was a British subject. Israel Ludlow filed damage claims of $255,000, and Frank Moss, retained by a Black committee, charged Devery, Thompson and Cooney. By September 10, Moss said, no policeman had been tried for clubbing.

The Tribune's front page, "WEST SIDE RACE RIOT. MOB ATTACKS NEGROES FOR POLICEMAN'S DEATH," named the victims and called Cooney's men "half-hearted." Its follow-ups, "POLICE BRUTAL TO A NEGRO" and "POLICE DEFY PEOPLE," made the police the story. Out of town the wire ran as "NEW YORK MOB AFTER NEGROES / Repetition of the Recent Riot in New Orleans," and another dispatch gave the police version of Lee's struggle as fact.

Black weeklies first reprinted the wire, the American Citizen adding "This Time It Is in the Heart of New York City." The Topeka Colored Citizen asked what Republicans would "say now of the North against the South" and later said the police "practically joined in." The Afro-American Advance saw "an epidemic of Negrophobia" spreading north from New Orleans.
As the campaign went on, Black papers blamed Tammany Hall; John E. Bruce, who had praised Devery in August, wrote that "the Tammany police are the real aggressors."

The Tribune had white men attack a passing youth first, a wire version said a Black man drew a revolver at a woman's remark, and the Sun blamed Spencer Walters. A dispatch in the Virginian-Pilot had Lee slash Kennedy unprovoked, the Tribune said he drew his weapons in self-defense, and the Sun reported David H. Tarr held on the stabbing charge.

reader.title: New York City race riot of August 1900
bases: White crowds, with police clubbing by several accounts, attacked Black people at random across a West Side district for a night in reprisal for one policeman's death (A2, A4, A22).
Independent local reports in the Tribune, Evening World and Sun and two separate wire accounts agree on the mob, the area, the beatings and the police role (A2, A6, A13, A14, A11).

accounts.label: New-York Tribune local report
accounts.gist: A drunken woman's outcry at Thorpe's wake led white men to beat a passing Black youth; the crowd then attacked Black people indiscriminately while Cooney's police were half-hearted and some encouraged it.

accounts.label: Wire report (police-side detail)
accounts.gist: A Black man drew a revolver at a woman's remark and the riot started; Lee slashed Kennedy, saying he was Thorpe's partner, and Kennedy shot him.

accounts.label: Sun court report
accounts.gist: Spencer Walters started the trouble by threatening two women; Tarr was held for stabbing Kennedy; the magistrate blamed white loafers.

accounts.label: Black complainants and their counsel
accounts.gist: Police did most of the clubbing, beat prisoners, dragged people from beds, and an officer had urged thugs to start trouble; the riot was 'a crusade' by policemen.

accounts.label: Colored Citizen (Topeka)
accounts.gist: About four hundred police practically joined the mob; none were killed and no arrests were made.

framing.detail: The Tribune headlined 'WEST SIDE RACE RIOT. MOB ATTACKS NEGROES FOR POLICEMAN'S DEATH', criticized the police, and later ran 'POLICE BRUTAL TO A NEGRO' and 'POLICE DEFY PEOPLE'.
Out-of-town papers ran the wire under headlines such as 'NEW YORK MOB AFTER NEGROES / Repetition of the Recent Riot in New Orleans'.
The Virginian-Pilot's 'THE POLICE WERE ACTIVE' dispatch gave the police account of Lee's attack on Kennedy as fact while describing a mob 'Seeking the Blood of Negroes'.
The Washington Evening Star centered Harris, 'UNDER CHARGE OF MURDER', with the riot as a sequel.
Early Black-press coverage reprinted the wire, the American Citizen adding 'This Time It Is in the Heart of New York City'.
Editors blamed the police and Tammany Hall, tied the riot to New Orleans and Northern mobs, and used it against the Democrats in the 1900 campaign.

info: Night of Wednesday, August 15, 1900, from about 11 p.m. until after 3 a.m. on August 16
West Side of Manhattan, centered on Eighth Ave. and 34th-37th Sts.; district from Twentieth (or Twenty-ninth) to Forty-second Sts., Sixth to Ninth Aves.; also Broadway and Sixth Ave. cars

Black residents and passers-by, among them Lloyd Lee (shot), Nathan Arlington, John B. Mallory, Alfred A. Akins, George Walker, Clarence Logan, Spencer Walters, Richard Williams, David H. Tarr, John Locket, James Wilson, William Richardson
No accusation against the victims as a group; the crowd sought vengeance because Arthur Harris, a Black man, was accused of stabbing Policeman Thorpe (Aug. 12)
White crowd of men and women from the neighborhood tenements and saloons; police clubbing of Black people reported by the Tribune, the Colored Citizen, Brooks and Moss
None reported; Lee called 'probably fatally hurt' on Aug. 16; the Colored Citizen said none were killed
By Sept. 10 no policeman had been tried for clubbing, per Moss; Police Board expected to reject his charges
